restrictions.note: No specialist-only or shared-care restriction stated in the lisinopril SmPC. Dual RAAS blockade, if absolutely necessary, only under specialist supervision (see cautions).

items.t: Usual starting dose 10 mg once daily. Usual maintenance 20 mg once daily; increase if needed after 2-4 weeks at a dose. Maximum used in long-term trials: 80 mg/day.

src.q: In patients with hypertension the usual recommended starting dose is 10 mg.
The usual effective maintenance dosage is 20 mg administered in a single daily dose.
if the desired therapeutic effect cannot be achieved in a period of 2 to 4 weeks on a certain dose level, the dose can be further increased.
The maximum dose used in long-term, controlled clinical trials was 80 mg/day.

items.t: Strongly activated renin-angiotensin system (renovascular hypertension, salt/volume depletion, cardiac decompensation, severe hypertension): start 2.5-5 mg under medical supervision.

src.q: A starting dose of 2.5-5 mg is recommended in such patients and the initiation of treatment should take place under medical supervision.

items.t: Already on a diuretic: if possible stop the diuretic 2-3 days before starting; if it cannot be stopped, start at 5 mg. Monitor renal function and serum potassium.

src.q: If possible, the diuretic should be discontinued 2 to 3 days before beginning therapy with Zestril.
In hypertensive patients in whom the diuretic cannot be discontinued, therapy with Zestril should be initiated with a 5 mg dose. Renal function and serum potassium should be monitored.

items.t: Start 2.5 mg once daily under medical supervision. Increase in steps of no more than 10 mg, at intervals of at least 2 weeks, to the highest tolerated dose, maximum 35 mg once daily.

src.q: Zestril may be initiated at a starting dose of 2.5 mg once a day, which should be administered under medical supervision to determine the initial effect on the blood pressure.
By increments of no greater than 10 mg At intervals of no less than 2 weeks To the highest dose tolerated by the patient up to a maximum of 35 mg once daily.

items.t: Start within 24 hours of symptoms only if systolic BP is at least 100 mmHg: 5 mg, then 5 mg after 24 hours, 10 mg after 48 hours, then 10 mg once daily for 6 weeks, then re-evaluate. Systolic BP 120 mmHg or lower in the first 3 days: 2.5 mg. Maintenance: reduce to 5 mg (temporarily 2.5 mg) if systolic BP 100 mmHg or lower; withdraw if systolic BP below 90 mmHg for more than 1 hour.

src.q: Treatment should not be started if systolic blood pressure is lower than 100 mm Hg.
The first dose of Zestril is 5 mg given orally, followed by 5 mg after 24 hours, 10 mg after 48 hours and then 10 mg once daily.
should be given a lower dose - 2.5 mg orally
If prolonged hypotension occurs (systolic blood pressure less than 90 mm Hg for more than 1 hour) Zestril should be withdrawn.
Treatment should continue for 6 weeks and then the patient should be re-evaluated.

items.t: 10 mg once daily, increased to 20 mg once daily if needed to reach a sitting diastolic BP below 90 mmHg.

src.q: the dose is 10 mg Zestril once daily which can be increased to 20 mg once daily, if necessary, to achieve a sitting diastolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg.

items.t: Elderly: use the renal table (CrCl) for the starting dose when age is linked with reduced renal function, then adjust to blood pressure.

src.q: When advanced age is associated with decrease in renal function, however, the guidelines set out in Table 1 should be used to determine the starting dose of Zestril.

items.t: Hypertension, 6-16 years: 20 to under 50 kg, start 2.5 mg once daily, maximum 20 mg daily; 50 kg or more, start 5 mg once daily, maximum 40 mg daily. Doses above 0.61 mg/kg (or above 40 mg) not studied.

src.q: The recommended initial dose is 2.5 mg once daily in patients 20 to <50 kg, and 5 mg once daily in patients ≥50 kg.
The dosage should be individually adjusted to a maximum of 20 mg daily in patients weighing 20 to <50 kg, and 40 mg in patients ≥50 kg.
Doses above 0.61 mg/kg (or in excess of 40 mg) have not been studied in paediatric patients

items.t: Not recommended under 6 years, in children with severe renal impairment (GFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²), or for indications other than hypertension. Consider a lower starting dose or longer interval in children with reduced renal function.

src.q: Zestril is not recommended in children below the age of 6, or in children with severe renal impairment (GFR < 30ml/min/1.73m2)
Zestril is not recommended in children in other indications than hypertension.
In children with decreased renal function, a lower starting dose or increased dosing interval should be considered.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to lisinopril, any excipient or any other ACE inhibitor.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to Zestril, to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1 or any other angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor.

items.t: History of angioedema with previous ACE inhibitor therapy; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

src.q: History of angioedema associated with previous ACE inhibitor therapy.
Hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.

items.t: With sacubitril/valsartan; do not start lisinopril within 36 hours of the last sacubitril/valsartan dose.

src.q: Zestril must not be initiated earlier than 36 hours after the last dose of sacubitril/valsartan

items.t: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy.

src.q: Second and third trimesters of pregnancy (see sections 4.4 and 4.6).

items.t: With aliskiren-containing products in patients with diabetes or renal impairment (GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m²).

items.t: Symptomatic hypotension: more likely with volume depletion (diuretics, salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea, vomiting), severe renin-dependent hypertension or heart failure. Monitor starting and dose changes closely in those at risk, including ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular disease.

src.q: hypotension is more likely to occur if the patient has been volume-depleted, e.g. by diuretic therapy, dietary salt restriction, dialysis, diarrhoea or vomiting, or has severe renin-dependent hypertension
In patients at increased risk of symptomatic hypotension, initiation of therapy and dose adjustment should be closely monitored.

items.t: Acute MI: must not be started if systolic BP 100 mmHg or lower or in cardiogenic shock. Do not start with renal dysfunction (serum creatinine above 177 micromol/l and/or proteinuria above 500 mg/24 h); consider withdrawal if creatinine rises above 265 micromol/l or doubles.

src.q: These are patients with systolic blood pressure of 100 mm Hg or lower, or those in cardiogenic shock.

treatment with Zestril should not be initiated in patients with evidence of renal dysfunction, defined as serum creatinine concentration exceeding 177 micromol/l and/or proteinuria exceeding 500 mg/24 h.
(serum creatinine concentration exceeding 265 micromol/l or a doubling from the pre-treatment value) then the physician should consider withdrawal of Zestril.

items.t: Mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: give with caution.

src.q: Zestril should be given with caution to patients with mitral valve stenosis and obstruction in the outflow of the left ventricle such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

items.t: Bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis to a single kidney: urea and creatinine may rise; start under close supervision with low doses and careful titration.

src.q: In these patients, treatment should be started under close medical supervision with low doses and careful dose titration.

items.t: Angioedema can occur at any time, including after months or years of treatment. Stop promptly; standard treatments for histamine-mediated angioedema may not work for bradykinin-mediated angioedema. Higher rate in black patients.

src.q: severe angioedema may also develop after months or years of long-term treatment with an ACE inhibitor. In such cases, Zestril should be discontinued promptly
standard therapies for histamine-mediated angioedema may be ineffective for bradykinin-mediated angioedema

items.t: History of angioedema not caused by an ACE inhibitor: may be at higher risk of angioedema on an ACE inhibitor (hereditary or idiopathic angioedema is a contraindication).

src.q: Patients with a history of angioedema unrelated to ACE inhibitor therapy may be at increased risk of angioedema while receiving an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: extreme caution in collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, allopurinol or procainamide, especially with renal impairment; check white cell counts periodically.

src.q: Zestril should be used with extreme caution in patients with collagen vascular disease, immunosuppressant therapy, treatment with allopurinol or procainamide
periodic monitoring of white blood cell counts is advised

items.t: Hyperkalaemia risk with renal impairment, diabetes, potassium supplements or salt substitutes, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole, aldosterone antagonists or ARBs. Monitor potassium and renal function.

src.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics and angiotensin-receptor blockers should be used with caution in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, and serum potassium and renal function should be monitored

items.t: Dual RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor with ARB or aliskiren) not recommended; if absolutely necessary only under specialist supervision with close monitoring. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor and ARB in diabetic nephropathy.

src.q: Dual blockade of RAAS through the combined use of ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers or aliskiren is therefore not recommended
ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers should not be used concomitantly in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

items.t: Diabetes on insulin or oral antidiabetics: monitor glycaemic control closely in the first month.

src.q: glycaemic control should be closely monitored during the first month of treatment with an ACE inhibitor

items.t: Hepatic failure (very rare): stop if jaundice or marked rise in liver enzymes.

src.q: Patients receiving Zestril who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue Zestril and receive appropriate medical follow-up.

items.t: Persistent dry cough can occur and resolves after stopping.

src.q: Characteristically, the cough is non-productive, persistent and resolves after discontinuation of therapy.

items.t: Major surgery or anaesthesia: hypotension can occur; correct with volume expansion.

src.q: If hypotension occurs and is considered to be due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion.

items.t: Anaphylactoid reactions with high-flux dialysis membranes (e.g. AN 69), LDL apheresis with dextran sulphate, and desensitisation (e.g. venom).

src.q: Anaphylactoid reactions have been reported in patients dialysed with high flux membranes (e.g. AN 69) and treated concomitantly with an ACE inhibitor.

items.t: Recent kidney transplant: no experience; not recommended.

src.q: There is no experience regarding the administration of Zestril in patients with recent kidney transplantation. Treatment with Zestril is therefore not recommended.

items.t: Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone), potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole: risk of significant hyperkalaemia, especially with renal impairment. Combination not recommended; if needed, use with caution and monitor potassium frequently.

src.q: Use of potassium sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, triamterene or amiloride), potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes, particularly in patients with impaired renal function, may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium.

Therefore, the combination of Zestril with the above-mentioned drugs is not recommended. If concomitant use is indicated, they should be used with caution and with frequent monitoring of serum potassium.

items.t: NSAIDs (including aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses): reduced antihypertensive effect; risk of worsening renal function, including acute renal failure, and raised potassium. Use with caution (especially in the elderly), keep hydrated and consider monitoring renal function.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs may lead to an increased risk of worsening of renal function, including possible acute renal failure, and an increase in serum potassium
The combination should be administered with caution, especially in the elderly.

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (insulin, oral agents): greater glucose lowering with risk of hypoglycaemia, mostly in the first weeks and in renal impairment.

src.q: may cause an increased blood glucose-lowering effect with risk of hypoglycaemia

items.t: Diuretics: additive effect; excessive BP fall when lisinopril is added, especially if the diuretic was started recently.

src.q: Patients already on diuretics and especially those in whom diuretic therapy was recently instituted, may occasionally experience an excessive reduction of blood pressure when Zestril is added.

items.t: Nitrates and other antihypertensives/vasodilators: additive falls in blood pressure. Lisinopril may be used with nitrates, aspirin at cardiac doses, thrombolytics and beta-blockers.

src.q: When Zestril is combined with other antihypertensive agents (e.g. glyceryl trinitrate and other nitrates, or other vasodilators), additive falls in blood pressure may occur.
Zestril may be used concomitantly with acetylsalicylic acid (at cardiologic doses), thrombolytics, beta-blockers and/or nitrates.

items.t: Sacubitril/valsartan: contraindicated (angioedema). mTOR inhibitors, racecadotril, vildagliptin, tissue plasminogen activator: higher angioedema risk.

src.q: Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with sacubitril/valsartan is contraindicated as this increases the risk of angioedema

items.t: Lithium: not recommended; if needed, monitor lithium levels carefully. Ciclosporin or heparin: monitor potassium.

src.q: Use of Zestril with lithium is not recommended, but if the combination proves necessary, careful monitoring of serum lithium levels should be performed
Hyperkalaemia may occur during concomitant use of ACE inhibitors with ciclosporin. Monitoring of serum potassium is recommended.

items.t: Starting dose by creatinine clearance: below 10 mL/min (including dialysis) 2.5 mg; 10-30 mL/min 2.5-5 mg; 31-80 mL/min 5-10 mg. Then titrate to blood pressure up to a maximum of 40 mg daily.

src.q: Dosage in patients with renal impairment should be based on creatinine clearance as outlined in Table 1 below.
Less than 10 ml/min (including patients on dialysis) 2.5 mg* 10-30 ml/min 2.5-5 mg 31-80 ml/min 5-10 mg
The dosage may be titrated upward until blood pressure is controlled or to a maximum of 40 mg daily.

items.t: Heart failure, MI and diabetic nephropathy: adjust the initial dose to creatinine clearance when below 80 mL/min.

src.q: In cases of renal impairment (creatinine clearance <80 ml/min), the initial Zestril dosage should be adjusted according to the patient's creatinine clearance (see Table 1).

items.t: SPS: seek specialist advice before starting if eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

items.t: SPS: some rise in creatinine is expected. Acceptable: creatinine rise under 50% above baseline (if below 266 micromol/L) or eGFR fall under 10% (if eGFR over 25). In CKD: eGFR fall over 25% or creatinine rise over 30% - look for other causes (e.g. volume depletion, NSAIDs); if none, stop or reduce to the previously tolerated dose.

src.q: An increase in serum creatinine of less than 50% above baseline, as long as it is less than 266 micromol/L, or a decrease in eGFR of less than 10% from baseline, as long as eGFR is over 25 mL/min/1.73 m2, can be considered as acceptable.
If no alternative cause is identified: Stop ACEI/ARB or reduce to previously tolerated dose

items.t: No hepatic dose adjustment stated. In cirrhosis, absorption fell about 30% but exposure rose about 50% (lower clearance).

src.q: Impairment of hepatic function in cirrhotic patients resulted in a decrease in lisinopril absorption (about 30% as determined by urinary recovery), but an increase in exposure (approximately 50%) compared to healthy subjects due to decreased clearance.

items.t: Very rarely ACE inhibitors cause cholestatic jaundice progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis; stop lisinopril if jaundice or marked liver enzyme rise.

src.q: Very rarely, ACE inhibitors have been associated with a syndrome that starts with cholestatic jaundice and progresses to fulminant necrosis and (sometimes) death.
Patients receiving Zestril who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue Zestril

items.t: SmPC: not recommended in the first trimester; contraindicated in the second and third trimesters. Stop as soon as pregnancy is diagnosed and switch if appropriate. If exposed from the second trimester, ultrasound check of fetal renal function and skull; watch the newborn for hypotension.

src.q: The use of ACE inhibitors is not recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy
The use of ACE inhibitors is contra-indicated during the second and third trimester of pregnancy
When pregnancy is diagnosed, treatment with ACE inhibitors should be stopped immediately, and, if appropriate, alternative therapy should be started.
Should exposure to ACE inhibitors have occurred from the second trimester of pregnancy, ultrasound check of renal function and skull is recommended.

items.t: MHRA: ACE inhibitors should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary, and only after discussing risks and benefits. On diagnosis of pregnancy, stop as soon as possible.

src.q: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists should not be used at any stage of pregnancy unless absolutely necessary
On diagnosis of pregnancy, treatment with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor antagonist should be stopped as soon as possible

items.t: BUMPS: early-pregnancy use is unlikely to harm the baby; use after about 20 weeks can cause oligohydramnios, fetal kidney damage, skull under-development, growth restriction, lung under-development and joint contractures, and may raise stillbirth risk. Extra monitoring is needed if continued after about 20 weeks.

src.q: Taking an ACE-I in early pregnancy is unlikely to harm your baby.
Taking an ACE-I after around 20 weeks of pregnancy can cause a number of problems in your baby
If you continue to take an ACE-I after around 20 weeks you will require additional monitoring to assess amniotic fluid levels and your baby's growth and wellbeing.

items.t: SmPC: no information; not recommended. Alternatives with better established safety are preferable, especially with a newborn or preterm infant.

src.q: Because no information is available regarding the use of Zestril during breast-feeding, Zestril is not recommended

items.t: MHRA (2009): lisinopril not recommended in breastfeeding; prefer alternatives, especially with a newborn or preterm baby. Clarification: not recommended but not absolutely contraindicated; may be prescribed if essential for the mother.

src.q: ramipril, lisinopril, fosinopril, trandolapril, moexipril, or perindopril: use in breastfeeding is not recommended
they are not absolutely contraindicated. Healthcare professionals may prescribe these medicines during breastfeeding if they consider that this treatment is essential for the lactating mother.

items.t: SPS (2023): lisinopril can be used with caution; enalapril is the preferred ACE inhibitor. Watch the infant for hypotension (drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, poor feeding, poor weight gain) and, in younger infants, for normal wet nappies. Neonates and infants under 2 months are at most risk.

src.q: Lisinopril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred.
In younger infants, monitor for normal urine production (wet nappies).
Neonates and infants less than 2 months are at the most risk from the side-effects of ACE inhibitors, particularly hypotension

items.t: Planning pregnancy: switch to an antihypertensive with an established pregnancy safety profile unless continued ACE inhibitor treatment is essential.

src.q: Unless continued ACE inhibitor therapy is considered essential, patients planning pregnancy should be changed to alternative anti-hypertensive treatments which have an established safety profile for use in pregnancy.
